Newly hatched Pacific-slope flycatcher chicks emerge from the egg at a remarkably modest size, with a wet mass at hatching of 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams]. This initial weight is quite small even among small passerines, reflecting the highly altricial state of the neonates at the moment of emergence. Field studies in coastal coniferous forests of the Pacific Northwest indicate that females typically lay a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], a relatively low annual reproductive frequency that is characteristic of many Empidonax species. The eggs, incubated primarily by the female, develop best under stable thermal conditions, and the incubation period culminates in hatching after an age at birth of approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days] when eggs are maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This developmental duration is consistent with values reported for other small tyrant flycatchers, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the relatively cool and wet conditions typical of the species' breeding habitat along the Pacific coast.

The nestling period is a phase of rapid morphological development, and the ultimate wet weight attained by adults is 10.9 grams [Wwi = 10.9 grams]. This adult mass represents a substantial increase from the hatching mass, representing a more than seven-fold increase in body size. During the post-hatching development, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning for their nutritional needs. Under typical field conditions, where ambient temperatures hover near the species' active metabolic optimum of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 16 days since birth [tx = 16 days since birth]. This comparatively brief nestling period is a hallmark of many aerial insectivores, potentially reducing the risk of nest predation during a vulnerable life stage. The rapid growth trajectory is fueled by a diet consisting almost exclusively of small flying insects, including flies, moths, and beetles, which are captured in sallying flights from exposed perches within the understory.

Sexual maturity is reached relatively quickly in this species, with the time since birth at puberty calculated at 48 days since birth [tp = 48 days since birth], a remarkably short interval for a temperate-zone passerine at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid maturation is possible only when individuals are operating under favorable thermal conditions, generally near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which supports high metabolic rates and efficient food processing. However, despite reaching gonadal development this early, most individuals do not breed in their first season. Instead, the time since birth at first brood is observed to be a full 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], meaning first-year birds delay reproduction until the following breeding season at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay is likely an adaptive response to the challenges of territory establishment and the acquisition of sufficient foraging experience. Furthermore, the initial wet weight of newly hatched individuals is recorded as 1.54 grams [Ww0 = 1.54 grams], a value that closely approximates the hatching mass but represents a more precise laboratory measurement of the freshly laid egg's contents.

The maximum reproductive rate of this species is inherently constrained by its single-brooded breeding strategy. Under optimal thermal conditions near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], females achieve their maximum potential output by producing a single clutch of approximately 3.5 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = approximately 3.5 eggs per nesting attempt]. This represents the highest possible fecundity per event, though in practice, clutch sizes at the upper end of this range are only realized when prey availability is exceptionally high during the early summer. The longevity of the Pacific-slope flycatcher is moderate for a passerine of its size; the maximum lifespan in the wild is recorded at approximately 6.9 years [am = approximately 6.9 years] when measured at an active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This figure is comparable to lifespans documented in other Empidonax species, such as the willow flycatcher, and suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes high annual survival over high annual reproductive output.

An interesting comparison emerges when examining the mass dynamics from hatching to adulthood. The wet weight at birth of 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams] is nearly identical to the measurement of initial wet weight obtained from calibrated laboratory scales, which recorded a value of 1.54 grams [Ww0 = 1.54 grams]. This slight discrepancy highlights the natural variation inherent in biological measurements, with the field-based figure reflecting a broader sample of wild nests. During the sensitive period around hatching, which occurs at an incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after an age at birth of about 14.5 days [ab = about 14.5 days], the embryos complete their organogenesis and yolk-sac resorption. Post-hatching, the nestlings grow rapidly to achieve the adult body mass of 10.9 grams [Wwi = 10.9 grams] before fledging at 16 days since birth [tx = 16 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Subsequent life-history events, including puberty at 48 days since birth [tp = 48 days since birth] and first reproduction at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], all occur under the species' characteristic thermal regime near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], underscoring the central role of temperature in pacing developmental milestones.
